section_path: Oil Producer organization extends production cuts
section_path_text: Oil Producer organization extends production cuts
text:
To nobody's surprise, OPEC extended its oil production cuts on November 30. The original cuts, which were agreed exactly one year ago on November 30, 2016, were for 6 months (January - June 2017) and were subsequently extended for 9 months (through March 2018). The new agreement will run through the end of 2018. The volume of the production adjustments remains the same: 1.2 million barrels per day (mb/d) for OPEC members and approximately 600,000 b/d for the participating non-OPEC countries led by Russia (300,000 b/d). According to the OPEC press release, "the market rebalancing has gathered pace since May, with the OECD stock overhang falling to around 140 million barrels (mb) above the five-year average for October, a drop of almost 140 mb since May. Moreover, crude in floating storage has also fallen significantly over this period. Despite this success, the Conference reiterated that it was vital that stock levels be drawn down to normal levels." The only real news in the OPEC announcement was that (a) Libya and Nigeria are being brought back into the fold and will be subject to production restrictions, and (b) that OPEC will review the current deal in June 2018 to consider "the opportunity for further adjustment actions". OPEC has not (yet) formulated a formal exit strategy, i.e. how to unwind the cuts when they are no longer needed. In the past, OPEC production quotas would gradually unravel as compliance by member states reduced. Time will tell if this agreement will be phased out differently.
Against the backdrop of healthy oil demand growth and reducing stocks (in absolute levels as well as in terms of days forward demand), this agreement seems to be positive for the oil markets and supportive of oil prices. What this deal means for the tanker market depends on a number of factors. As we discussed in a tanker opinion last month (" Tanker Market Hits Peak Supply Growth "), the outlook for tanker supply growth in 2018 is more subdued compared to 2017 and the key driver for shipping rates will be growth in ton-mile demand.
The outlook for global oil demand in 2018 is fairly robust. The IEA expects world oil demand to grow by 1.3 mb/d in 2018, compared to 1.6 mb/d this year.

text:
As we are approaching the end of 2017, a year most tanker owners would probably rather forget as soon as possible, we want to look forward to 2018, in particular focusing on some of the key elements that will drive tanker demand: oil demand growth and refining expansion. How much more oil will the world need, where will they need it, who will supply the crude and where will it be refined? We already discussed in last week's opinion (" No Surprise From OPEC ") that, as long as OPEC maintains its productions cuts, most of the incremental crude oil in 2018 will likely be light tight oil coming from the U.S.
In terms of refining capacity growth, there is always a mix of new greenfield refining projects on the one hand and upgrading capacity and efficiency improvements on the other hand. As a result of heightened environmental regulations and a sustained lower crude oil price environment (which led to a "lower forever" outlook of many people in the oil industry), most expansions involve upgrades and debottlenecking of existing facilities, rather than new refineries.
However, there are still a number of greenfield refineries that are expected to start operating in 2018. To name a few examples: In Vietnam, the 200,000 b/d Nghi Son refinery is getting ready to start up. Kuwait's national oil company KPC is a partner in the project and Kuwait will provide a significant portion of the crude for the refinery. Test cargoes started to arrive earlier this year. In Canada, the 50,000 b/d Sturgeon refinery in Redwater, Alberta will enter its first full year of operation. This is the first such refinery built in Canada in more than 30 years. The Sturgeon refinery is small and will use domestic crude and sell its products locally, so it has a minimal impact on trade-flows. Another new refinery which will have only a limited impact on crude oil and product tradeflows is the Star refinery that Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR is building in Turkey. Not surprisingly, this 200,000+ b/d refinery will mainly run Azeri crude, although it will also source crude from Russia and Kirkuk crude from Iraq. Most of the refined product output is expected to stay in Turkey. In Poland, Grupa LOTUS is upgrading/expanding their refinery in Gdansk. This will add 100-150,000 b/d of capacity in 2018.

Growth of only 0.1 Mb/d in the Middle East and China, with 0.2 Mb/d of expansion in the U.S. and Canada.

section_path: Oil reform creates opportunities for tankers
section_path_text: Oil reform creates opportunities for tankers
text:
In December 2013, Mexico made the necessary changes to its constitution to allow a widespread reform of the country's energy sector. Until that time, in the oil, gas and power sectors, Mexico was a largely closed and monopoly-driven energy market, lacking in investment and productivity growth. The reform package, introduced by President Enrique Pena Nieto has bolstered long-term growth through increased efficiency and productivity.
Mexico used to be one of the world's major oil producers and exporters, but its position has weakened over the years. According to the IEA, oil production declined by one-third from a peak of 3.8 million barrels per day (mb/d) in 2004 to 2.5 mb/d in 2016. In 2017, Mexico's production continued its steady decline. By October, crude oil output was down to 2.18 mb/d. The declines in Mexican production have been largely the result of underinvestment in the sector by the state-owned monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (PEMEX). They lacked the resources to slow declines in mature fields or to develop new ones. PEMEX also did not have the technical capacity to bring new production online from deep-water and shale resources. Although 2018 is expected to be another challenging year, the IEA expects that Mexican oil production will turn around in future years as foreign investment in the sector, resulting from the energy reforms, will start to bear fruit. A series of bidding rounds that began in 2015 opened the sector to private investment and is bringing the necessary technology to develop new projects, including tight oil. The IEA projects that Mexican oil production will turn around and can reach 3.4 mb/d in 2040.
The impact of the challenges in Mexico's oil industry on the tanker market has been profound, although not in ways you may expect. Declines in oil production have previously led to cuts in crude oil exports and reduced crude tanker employment, in particular for Aframaxes in the Caribbean and the Atlantic Basin. In recent years exports have stabilized, despite falling production, which implies reductions in domestic crude oil demand. The impact on the tanker market comes from the changes in the destination. The traditional export market for Mexican crude was the United States; back in 2014 71% of Mexico's crude landed in the U.S. These short-haul voyages had a limited impact on crude oil tanker employment.

In 2017 to date, the market share of the U.S. in Mexico's crude oil exports has been down to 50%. The growth market has been Asia, which now imports 27% of Mexico's crude exports, up from 9% in 2014. The main beneficiaries of this shift have been the VLCCs, which transport 70% of the Asian volumes, with the remaining 30% going on Suezmaxes. As domestic crude oil production in the U.S. goes from strength to strength, this trend towards diverting more Mexican exports to Asia is expected to continue, which will further support long-haul VLCC movements from the Caribbean to the Pacific.
Despite being a significant crude oil producer and exporter, Mexico is also a net importer of refined oil products because PEMEX failed to invest enough funds in the domestic refining industry. Mexico's refining challenges caused a rapid increase in product imports, predominantly sourced from the U.S. Mexico's petroleum product imports more than doubled over the last 10 years. The two key commodities are gasoline (65%) and diesel (25%). According to the U.S. Energy Information Agency, Mexico is by far the largest export destination for U.S. gasoline. In 2017, more than half (55%) of U.S. gasoline exports end up south of the border. The vast majority of this product is moved via seaborne trade. We are not aware of any product pipelines (other than LPG) between the U.S. and Mexico, and only small volumes of gasoline are transported by rail.
The Mexican oil industry continues to face challenges, but the outlook for the country's crude oil and product trades is supportive for the tanker market.

section_title: Pipeline outage shuffles crude oil trade in the North Sea
section_path: Pipeline outage shuffles crude oil trade in the North Sea
section_path_text: Pipeline outage shuffles crude oil trade in the North Sea
text:
On Monday 11 December, the Forties Pipeline System (FPS) in the North Sea was closed for repairs. The 235-mile pipeline transports about 450,000 barrels of oil per day (b/d) on average, which is about 40% of UK production. It is one of the oldest pipeline systems in the North Sea. It started operating in the Forties field in 1975 and links 85 North Sea oil and gas fields to facilities on the UK mainland, including the Hound Point export terminal and the 201,000 b/d Grangemouth refinery. BP originally operated the Forties oil and gas field, the pipeline and the refinery. It sold its interest in the oil field to Apache in 2003 and Ineos bought the Grangemouth refinery and chemical plant in 2005. Earlier this year, Ineos also bought the FPS from BP for a reported $250 million. The FPS is not expected to reopen until January 2018 and in this Weekly Opinion we will assess the potential impact on the tanker markets of this significant disruption.
To determine the impact of the pipeline closure on the tanker market, we must evaluate how much crude oil is exported from Hound Point (the export terminal for Forties crude in Scotland) and what type of vessels are used. Over the last 4 years (for which we have detailed data), exports have increasingly favored VLCCs. This shift came largely at the expense of Aframaxes. Suezmax tankers are only being used occasionally for exports from Hound Point. Total shipments from Hound Point have averaged about 300 Kb/d for the last three years.
In 2014, 66% of the cargoes loaded in Hound Point were on Aframax tankers as most of the voyages were headed to countries in Europe such as the Netherlands (Rotterdam), Germany (Wilhelmshaven and Brunsbüttel) and the UK (Fawley and Stanlow). Since then, Asian destinations have become much more important, and in 2017 to date they accounted for 67% of the volumes loaded in Hound Point. China and Korea each import more than 30% of these volumes. Exports to China increased after Chinese oil companies acquired interests in several North Sea fields bringing their share of production to about 200,000 b/d.

As a result, VLCCs are now the main size class used for shipments from Hound Point which is now the largest VLCC load port in the UKC area. Other large load locations are Rotterdam and Southwold, used for Ship-to-Ship transfers.
The shift from short haul moves to long haul exports to Asia has been a great development for Hound Point-related ton mile demand, which nearly tripled from 2014 to 2017.
The unexpected closure of the pipeline led to a reduction of about 450 Kb/d of light sweet crude from the global market. This initially caused the price of Brent crude oil to increase by about $1.54 from Friday Dec. 8 to Monday Dec. 11 and WTI, another light sweet crude, increased by $0.63 during this period. The Brent-Dubai spread also increased from $3.50 to $4.25, reflecting the perceived shortage of light, sweet crude versus the heavier Dubai variety, making Middle Eastern crudes more attractive.
It is too early to have definitive statistics but anecdotal evidence suggests that Chinese buyers have increased their purchases from West Africa while Korean buyers have focused more on the Middle Eastern suppliers. U.S. crude oil also became more attractive as the Brent - WTI spread widened further.
Aframax rates in the North Sea increased by 7.5 points on the day that the closure was announced. The impact on other freight rates was less immediate and it is harder to link them to the pipeline repairs. The upcoming Christmas weekend affects rates as well.
Yesterday, Ineos (the operator of the pipeline) announced that they anticipate that the pipeline will be back online in early January. Unless there are unforeseen delays, the impact over the coming weeks will likely be relatively subdued as the market slows down for the holiday season.
